AM9A-02.note: Asks for 2x, not x; 9 is the x-trap. Fine, but this is the standard ACT twist.

AM9A-04.note: Strictly this is arithmetic-undefined at x=5; wording is standard ACT.

AM9A-05.note: x=5, y=7, y-x=2. -2 is the x-y trap.

AM9A-06.note: 16-36+c=0. Factors as (x-4)(x-5), so x=4 really is a root.

AM9A-07.note: k=48; y=48/16=3. Doubling x quarters y.

AM9A-09.note: k=6 gives 6x-3=6x+7, contradiction. Note k=6 is also the only value that could give infinitely many solutions if the constants matched; they do not (-3 vs 7), so NO solution is unambiguous.

AM9A-10.note: 10x+18=68. The two decimal options are sign-error traps on the -2(x-5).

AM9A-11.note: (w+2)(w+2)=w(w+5); w=4, original 4x9=36, new 6x6=36. The w^2 cancels so it stays linear.

AM9A-12.note: Cross-multiply; x=14 is in neither excluded domain (2, -6).

AM9A-14.note: Both the linear coefficient (a-3=2) and the constant (-3a=-15) give a=5, so the identity is genuinely consistent.

AM9A-15.note: 3k/5k, (3k+12)/5k=9/10, k=8, blue=5k=40. 8 (the multiplier) and 24 (red) are the traps.

AM9A-16.note: Exponent is parenthesised in the render, so no 3^x+2 vs 3^(x+2) ambiguity. 49 is the 7^2 trap.

AM9A-17.note: b+c=16, b-c=12, c=2, b=14. 14 (boat speed) is the trap.

AM9A-18.note: -4<n<8, so n=-3..7 = 11 integers. 13 is the inclusive-endpoint count. Strict inequalities plus an integer count is a genuinely late-form item.

AM9A-19.note: (x+y)^2=400=234+2xy so xy=83. The two numbers are 10 +/- sqrt(17) - irrational. A student who tries to find the numbers instead of using the identity is stuck, which is the point, but it is worth knowing the item has no integer solution pair. 166 is the forgot-to-halve trap.

AM9A-20.note: l+w=23, lw=120 gives 15 and 8. 8 (shorter side) and 11.5 (half-perimeter) are the traps.

AM9A-21.note: x=8, x^2=64. The 'x is a positive number' clause is redundant - the linear equation has the single root 8 - but it does no harm. 8 is the answered-the-wrong-quantity trap.

AM9A-23.note: Factor theorem: f(2)=4+4a=0. Synthetic division gives the same.

AM9A-24.note: (x-y)(x+y)=40 so x+y=10; x=7, y=3. 10 (the sum) and 7 (x) are the traps.

AM9A-25.note: 0.25(12-d)+d=6, d=4. Classic drain-and-replace; the common wrong model (just adding antifreeze without draining) is the reason this is hard.

AM9A-26.note: a+2b=10 with a-b=1 gives b=3, a=4. TYPOGRAPHY: the prompt writes the multiplication as a literal 'x' ('2^a x 4^b') in a batch where x is the variable everywhere else. It resolves only because reading it as a third unknown makes the item unsolvable. Should be a dot or an asterisk.

AM9A-27.note: Rate 375/25=15/guest, fee 260. 260+15g<=1500 gives g<=82.67, so 82. 83 is the round-up trap and is the only near-miss in the batch; the item is sound because 'at most $1,500' forces the floor.

AM9A-28.note: n^2 cancels, 5n+4=7n-30, n=17; not an excluded value (3, -1).
